opus-5.5.text:
I think what's significant is that it gets at the difference between pattern matching and actually executing a procedure. When we give a model a few demonstrations of, say, multi-digit addition, there are two very different things it could be doing. It could be picking up surface-level correlations, like "inputs that look like this tend to produce outputs that look like that," or it could be internalizing the steps of the algorithm and then carrying them out on whatever input it sees. Those two can look identical on in-distribution examples, but they come apart as soon as you go outside what the demonstrations cover: longer numbers, different lengths, edge cases like long carry chains.

So when a model can take an algorithm described in context and apply it correctly to examples that are structurally different from the ones it was shown, that's evidence it's doing something closer to following a procedure. That matters because so much of what we care about in reasoning is exactly that kind of systematic generalization. We don't want a model that has memorized what a correct answer usually looks like. We want one that can reliably carry out a sequence of operations it hasn't seen in that exact form.

It's also significant because it suggests the bottleneck isn't always the model's capacity, but how we communicate the task. In our work on algorithmic prompting, a lot of the gains came from being very explicit, spelling out every step, every carry, every intermediate state, so there was less room for the model to latch onto the wrong interpretation. When you remove that ambiguity, models that seemed to fail at length generalization suddenly do much better. That tells us something about in-context learning: the model can pick up fairly precise behaviors from context, but it needs the right kind of signal.

And finally, there's a compositional angle. Once a model can reliably execute one algorithm from context, you can start asking whether it can call that skill as a subroutine inside a bigger task, whether learned skills can be composed. To me that's where it gets really exciting, because that's much closer to how we think about general reasoning: building complex behavior out of reliable, reusable pieces.

r001.rationale: The response says a model should carry out the same algorithm on structurally different inputs beyond its demonstrations, including longer numbers and edge cases.

r002.rationale: It mentions composing reusable skills into larger tasks, but does not propose progressively teaching models by building on learned skills or compare this to school students.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what's really interesting about it is that it gets at the question of whether these models are actually learning something general versus just memorizing. When you show a model a few examples of an algorithm, say a simple arithmetic procedure or a string manipulation rule, and it can then apply that algorithm to inputs it's never seen, and especially to inputs that are longer or structurally different from the demonstrations, that tells you something beyond pattern matching is happening. It suggests the model has extracted some kind of procedural representation of the task, not just a lookup over the examples you gave it.

And I think the reason that matters is that it's a form of generalization that's very different from what we usually measure. Most of our benchmarks test whether a model can do well on test examples drawn from the same distribution as training. But applying an algorithm to new examples is more like compositional or systematic generalization. You're asking, did the model learn the rule, or did it learn the instances? Humans do this pretty effortlessly. If I teach you how to add two numbers with three digits, you can add numbers with ten digits. That's actually a surprisingly high bar for neural networks historically, and a lot of the work on length generalization shows that models often fail at exactly this kind of thing.

So when a language model does succeed at it, even partially, it's significant because it's evidence that in-context learning isn't just retrieving a memorized skill from pretraining. The model is, in some sense, executing a procedure that was specified at inference time. And when it fails, that's equally informative, because it tells us where the boundary is between understanding the algorithm and approximating its outputs. I find that boundary to be one of the most useful places to look if you want to understand what these models are really doing.

r001.rationale: The response says a model should apply an algorithm from demonstrations to unseen inputs, including longer or structurally different ones, and frames this as learning the rule rather than the instances.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose progressively teaching models by building on skills they have already learned, or compare that approach to students learning in school.

astra-6.text:
I think the significant thing is that it suggests the model has learned something more general than the particular examples it was shown. If it can apply an algorithm to a new input, then it’s doing more than reproducing an answer from a demonstration—it’s picking up a procedure that can be reused.

But there are different degrees of generalization. A new example might still be very similar to the demonstrations. A stronger test is whether the model can handle longer inputs, or inputs with a different structure, where the same procedure should still work. That helps us distinguish between learning patterns that happen to give the right answers and learning something closer to the algorithm itself.

What makes that interesting to me is the possibility that a model can use examples to infer how to solve a task, rather than needing demonstrations that cover every case. The important question is how reliably that behavior extends beyond the setting in which we observed it.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can reuse the same procedure on new inputs, including longer inputs or inputs with different structures beyond the demonstrations.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose progressively teaching models by building on previously learned skills or compare this to students in school.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s significant is that it helps us distinguish between memorizing examples and learning a procedure. If a model can apply an algorithm to inputs that differ from its demonstrations, that’s evidence that it has picked up something more general about the task.

But a lot depends on what we mean by “new.” A model might succeed on new examples of the same length and then fail when the inputs get longer. So I’d be careful about treating a few successful examples as proof that it has learned the algorithm. The interesting question is how systematically that ability generalizes, and where it breaks down.

r001.rationale: It says the model can apply an algorithm to inputs that differ from its demonstrations, distinguishing procedure learning from memorization.

r002.rationale: It does not propose progressively teaching models by building on previously learned skills or compare this to school students.
